title: Values, names and output

curriculum.title: Values, Names, and Output
curriculum.answer:
A variable name refers to a value. Assignment evaluates the right side and binds the name on the left to that value; it does not automatically make a separate copy of an object. Printing shows the value currently referred to by a name. Reassignment changes that binding.

### Assignment gives a value a name

Think of a variable name as a label attached to a value. The name is on the left, and `=` binds it to the value produced by the right side. The value can be text in quotes, a whole number, or a decimal number.

```python
name = "Sam"
print(name)
```
```text
Sam
```

Here `"Sam"` is the starting value. The first line stores it in `name`. The second line prints the current contents of `name`, so `Sam` appears.

### Printing shows the current value

`print` displays values on the screen. You can print a value directly, or print a name to display whatever was stored there. To understand a later print, follow which value the name currently refers to.

```python
count = 4
count = 7
print(count)
```
```text
7
```

The first line puts `4` in `count`. The second line replaces it with `7`. The name `count` no longer refers to `4`. Printing then shows `7`.

### Common mistakes

`=` means assignment, not a check for equality. `count = 4` stores `4`; it does not ask a question. Names also matter exactly: `copy_name` and `nickname2` are different names. Using a name before anything is assigned to it causes a `NameError`. Reassignment is normal, but every name must be assigned before it is printed.
